title: Global Misinformation Spillovers in the Vaccination Debate Before and During the COVID-19 Pandemic: Multilingual Twitter Study
screen_reason: Observational multilingual Twitter study (316 million vaccine-related tweets, 18 languages, October 2019 - March 2021, users geolocated to 28 countries). It reports shares of shared/retweeted URLs whose domains appear on low-credibility domain lists, with stated denominators: 26% for users in no-vax communities versus 2.4% for other users, and 14% falling to 7% for URLs retweeted from the United States. These are SHARING content shares (% of shared links that are unreliable), which the instructions place under SHARING rather than CONTENT. Not an intervention or detection study; the classifier-free ground truth is a published domain list.

estimates.country: Countries speaking English, Italian, French or Greek among the 28 geolocated countries (Australia, Canada, France, Great Britain, Greece, Ireland, Italy, New Zealand, United States)
estimates.date: October 2019 - March 2021 (four 3-month windows: Oct-Dec 2019, Jul-Sep 2020, Oct-Dec 2020, Jan-Mar 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of domains shared by users in no-vax communities that appear on lists of known low-credibility domains
estimates.value_raw: 26% of the domains shared by no-vax communities came from lists of known low-credibility domains (vs 2.4% for other users, P<.001)
estimates.denominator: All domains shared by users belonging to communities labelled no-vax, within the vaccine-keyword tweet corpus, restricted to countries whose language has a low-credibility domain list (English, Italian, French, Greek); the count of domains is not reported
estimates.definition: A shared domain counted in the numerator if it appears on the compiled list of 1732 low-credibility domains; classification is at the level of the website, not the individual tweet or claim
estimates.misinfo_def: No definitional sentence; misinformation is operationalised through source credibility - 'the quality of the cited URL domains is often used as a gauge of the quality of the tweet's content [35,36]. In this study, we used a similar approach by combining lists of low-credibility domains from several languages and countries.'
estimates.n: not reported (domains shared by users in no-vax communities; the reconstructed retweet and cosharing networks contain 2.7 million users in total)
estimates.source_quote: The difference is remarkable: 26% of the domains shared by no-vax communities came from lists of known low-credibility domains versus only 2.4% of those cited by the other users came from lists of known low-credibility domains (P<.001).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Characterizing the Users in No-Vax Communities', p.7; Figure 4D
estimates.ground_truth_detail: A list of 1732 low-credibility domains compiled from Bufale (Italian), Wikipedia's 'List of fake news websites' (English), Media Bias/Fact Check (English), Le Monde (French) and dwrean.net (Greek). No list existed for the other seven languages, which the authors say makes their misinformation flows 'a lower bound'. Community membership (no-vax vs other) came from hierarchical clustering of retweet networks plus two rounds of manual tweet annotation by 12 annotators with vaccine-debate background; Cohen kappa = 0.84 for pro-vax vs no-vax, 0.51 for the 3-class task in round 1 and 0.64 in round 2; clustering robustness checks gave 0.90-0.95 agreement with alternative algorithms
estimates.moderator_quote: We began by assembling a list of vaccine-related words translated into 18 different languages (vaccine, novax, measles, MMR, vaccinated, etc), obtaining a set of 459 keywords [...] Following the previous literature on misinformation tracking [44,45], we collected a list of low-credibility domains. As sources of low-credibility websites, we relied on Bufale (Italian) [46], Wikipedia (English) [47], Media Bias/Fact-Check (English) [48], Le Monde (French) [49], and dwrean (Greek) [50], obtaining a list of 1732 domains.
estimates.notes: SUBGROUP-BY-DESIGN row: the no-vax vs other-user contrast is the paper's headline finding, not an incidental demographic split, so both halves are recorded (see the companion 2.4% row). This is a within-antivaccination-community figure and must not be read as a platform-wide prevalence. Two denominator ambiguities an adjudicator should note: (1) it is not stated whether the base is unique domains or domain-shares (Figure 4D is captioned 'proportion of low-credibility domains shared by users', and the text says 'domains shared', so a per-share reading is not certain); (2) the figure averages over countries and over the four periods, and only the four languages with a domain list contribute. year is set to 2020 as the midpoint of an Oct 2019 - Mar 2021 collection window.

estimates.denominator: All domains shared by users in the vaccine-debate retweet/cosharing networks who are NOT in a community labelled no-vax, restricted to countries whose language has a low-credibility domain list (English, Italian, French, Greek); the count of domains is not reported
estimates.definition: A shared domain counted in the numerator if it appears on the compiled list of 1732 low-credibility domains; classification at website level
estimates.misinfo_def: No definitional sentence; misinformation is operationalised through source credibility - 'the quality of the cited URL domains is often used as a gauge of the quality of the tweet's content [35,36]. estimates.n: not reported (domains shared by users outside no-vax communities)
estimates.source_quote: The difference is remarkable: 26% of the domains shared by no-vax communities came from lists of known low-credibility domains versus only 2.4% of those cited by the other users came from lists of known low-credibility domains (P<.001).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Characterizing the Users in No-Vax Communities', p.7; Figure 4D
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 1732-domain low-credibility list (Bufale, Wikipedia, Media Bias/Fact Check, Le Monde, dwrean.net); same community-labelling pipeline (hierarchical Paris clustering of retweet networks, 8000 tweets annotated in round 1 by 12 annotators, 820 in round 2; Cohen kappa 0.84 pro-vax vs no-vax, 0.51 and 0.64 for the 3-class task)
estimates.moderator_quote: Note that low-credibility domains were collected only in Italian, French, English, and Greek; therefore, the plots refer to countries speaking these languages. No-Vax: discrediting vaccines. Other: non-discrediting vaccines.
estimates.notes: This is the comparison half of the paper's headline contrast and is the closer of the two to a general prevalence figure: it is the low-credibility share of link-sharing among ordinary participants in the vaccine debate on Twitter. Still not a platform-wide figure - the corpus is a vaccine-keyword corpus, so the base is vaccine-related link sharing only. Same unique-domains-vs-domain-shares ambiguity as the companion row.

estimates.date: Vaccine development period, 1 October - 31 December 2020 (representative point; the same measure falls to 7% in the vaccine rollout period, 1 January - 31 March 2021)
estimates.measure_type: % of the URLs retweeted from the United States in the vaccine debate whose domains are low-credibility
estimates.value_raw: the proportion of low-credibility domains in the URLs retweeted from the United States dropped from 14% to 7%
estimates.denominator: All URLs retweeted from United States accounts within the vaccine-keyword Twitter corpus during the vaccine development period (Oct-Dec 2020); the count is not reported
estimates.definition: URL counted in the numerator if its domain appears on the 1732-domain low-credibility list
estimates.misinfo_def: No definitional sentence; misinformation is operationalised as links to domains on published low-credibility/fake-news website lists
estimates.n: not reported (URLs retweeted from the United States)
estimates.source_quote: Note that Twitter's account purge substantially impacted the misinformation spread worldwide: the proportion of low-credibility domains in the URLs retweeted from the United States dropped from 14% to 7%.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Cross-Border Information Spillover in the Global Vaccination Debate', p.9
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 1732-domain low-credibility list assembled from Bufale, Wikipedia, Media Bias/Fact Check, Le Monde and dwrean.net; English-language lists apply to the US case
estimates.moderator_quote: Finally, we focused on misinformation flows across countries by considering the fraction of low-credibility domains imported per country (Figure 6C), that is, the fraction of tweets pointing to low-credibility URLs, over the total number of RTs from one country to another.
estimates.notes: TIME SERIES COLLAPSED to the vaccine development period (Oct-Dec 2020) value of 14%; the paired post-moderation value is 7% in the vaccine rollout period (Jan-Mar 2021), after the January 2021 account suspensions. The pre-purge point was chosen as representative because it precedes the exogenous platform-moderation shock the paper is measuring; an adjudicator preferring an end-of-window value should substitute 7%. borderline=true because the denominator wording is ambiguous between all URLs retweeted from US accounts and the cross-border subset only - the surrounding paragraph discusses cross-border retweets ('46% of cross-border RTs of US users linked to low-credibility websites in the vax development period came from accounts that were suspended'), so the base may be cross-border retweets rather than all US retweets.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen but NOT extracted, with reasons: (1) '68% of all the low-credibility URLs retweeted worldwide came from the United States (average over the 4 periods), a proportion much higher than the total volume of URLs (42%) retweeted from the United States' - this is a concentration-of-origin statement (one country of 28 accounting for 68% of low-credibility retweets while accounting for 42% of all retweeted URL volume). I did NOT create a CONCENTRATION row because R1 requires conc_group_pct to be the group as a percentage of USERS OR SOURCES, and no such figure exists here: the 42% is a share of activity, not a share of sources, so pairing it with the 68% would misrepresent the group-size axis. FLAGGED FOR ADJUDICATION - if the review accepts an activity-share as the group axis, the row would be conc_unit=source, conc_dimension=sharing, conc_group_label='United States (1 of 28 countries; 42% of all retweeted URL volume)', conc_share_pct=68. Related figures in the same paragraph: US share of low-credibility URLs fell from 74% (vaccine development) to 55% (vaccine rollout); 46% of cross-border RTs of US users linking to low-credibility sites came from accounts later suspended; the share of low-credibility URLs reaching Latin American countries that originated in Russia rose from 1% to 18% - all of these have a misinformation-only denominator (within-misinfo composition), so none is a prevalence. (2) 'Proportion of users in no-vax communities with respect to the size of the RT networks (average in the 4 periods: 16.9% [SD 0.18], 30.9% [SD 0.18], 23.1% [SD 0.14], and 13.7% [SD 0.12])' - tempting as a REACH figure since the authors call these 'communities where users were substantially exposed to no-vax content', but the denominator is users in a vaccine-keyword retweet network (not a population, which the REACH rule requires), community membership is a clustering artefact rather than measured exposure, an antivaccination STANCE is not verified falsity, and the cross-country SDs are as large as the means. Excluded under R4. (3) Figure 3A 'Proportion of tweets labeled as no-vax' - no numeric value appears in the text, only a figure, and again stance is not veracity. (4) Suspended-account shares (13.3% in no-vax communities vs 1.8% among others; US suspensions rising from 38% to 77% around 1 January 2021; 89% of suspended US users belonged to the no-vax community) - platform enforcement outcomes, not misinformation content shares; the authors themselves concede 'we cannot be certain that the accounts indeed were sharing harmful content'. (5) RWC polarization scores (0.94, 0.84, 0.76, 0.73) and NMI values (0.27 vs 0.22; 0.15 vs 0.33) - network-structure metrics, not prevalence. (6) Corpus-validity check on 300 tweets (7% pet-related, 6% non-relevant) - measurement noise, not misinformation. (7) Geolocation coverage (48.7% of users geolocated; 14.9 million users = 39.4% of the data set) - sample construction. No RECALL, EXPOSURE, CONTENT or QUALITY rows are derivable: nothing measures what individuals consumed or a share of items judged true/false against a claim-level ground truth.

rob.design: Large observational platform study: 316 million vaccine-related tweets in 18 languages collected in real time through the Twitter Streaming API using 459 translated keywords, October 2019 - March 2021, analysed in four 3-month windows. Users geolocated by matching profile location strings to GeoNames (48.7% geolocated; countries with >2000 unique users per period retained, giving 28 countries in 11 languages; 14.9 million geolocated users, 39.4% of the corpus). Retweet and cosharing networks per country-period, Paris hierarchical clustering, then two rounds of manual annotation (8000 tweets by 12 annotators with vaccine-debate expertise and language competence, then 820 popular tweets) to label communities no-vax; Cohen kappa 0.84 for the pro-vax/no-vax distinction, 0.51 for the 3-class task in round 1 and 0.64 in round 2; robustness against Louvain and alternative cutoffs gives 0.90-0.95 concordance. Misinformation ground truth is a 1732-domain low-credibility list from five published sources, available only in English, Italian, French and Greek, so estimates are explicitly a lower bound. No response rate applies. Author-acknowledged biases: Twitter users are not representative (more educated, urban, younger, male), Twitter penetration differs by country so cross-country comparisons are cautioned against, edges of weight 1 were filtered in the largest networks, no bot detection was performed, and no spelling-error handling. A relevance check on 300 random tweets found 7% pet-related and 6% non-relevant.
